recentItems.title: Mike D: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Robin Hilton | November 20, 2026
When news broke earlier in the year that Mike D of the Beastie Boys had a new album on the way, it felt historic. It was the first-ever solo release from any member of the group, and the first new music at all from that universe since Adam Yauch (aka MCA) died in 2012. Thank You is bristling with reflections on the vast mysteries of life. The beats and bars hit hard before giving way to waves of reverb-soaked sweetness and even vulnerability, with an overwhelming sense of gratitude as the anchor.

Much of the vocals on Thank You are filtered through a swirling wash of effects, but here at the Desk, Mike D drops bars completely unadorned and in the clear. He and the band — which includes his sons, Skylar and Davis Diamond, on electronics — focus entirely on the new album, opening with "Make It Stop," a glitchy commentary on the age of self-destructive naval gazing. They follow with the meditative "I Don't Care," the hooky lead-off single "Switch Up" and "It's Time," a punchy, playful call to seek higher truths and take action.

"Time really flies by when you do these things," Mike D tells the NPR crowd before the group closes with "Thank You," a wistful look back at the wondrous magic of youth. "I guess we are having fun, then."

recentItems.title: Tove Lo: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Stephen Thompson | November 18, 2026
Tove Lo isn’t the biggest pop star in the world, but few can boast the depth, range and consistency of her catalog. “Habits (Stay High)” and “Talking Body,” two career-making blockbuster singles from her 2014 debut Queen of the Clouds, do a nice job establishing the breadth of her talent, with the former exuding melancholy and the latter luxuriating in the hedonism of love. (Between songs at the Tiny Desk, she refers to “Talking Body” as “the banger no one believed in.”) Creatively speaking, the Swedish singer has been on a tear ever since.

For her too-long-awaited Tiny Desk debut, Tove Lo picks an impeccable cross-section of her catalog, alternating the aforementioned smashes with incredible newer material. “source of life,” which closes her marvelous new album ESTRUS, opens this set with a song that would have fit right in on her under-heralded 2022 gem Dirt Femme. And, in a move engineered to placate the listeners discerning enough to hail Dirt Femme as a pre-midlife dirtbag masterpiece, she includes one of that album’s greatest songs, “No One Dies from Love.” 

This Tiny Desk set has it all: a banger with a mournful side, a banger about getting it on, a banger that shows she’s still got it and a banger that doubles as catnip for the hopefully ever-growing Dirt Femme Hive. What more could you possibly need, besides about 20 more fantastic Tove Lo songs? If she’d played all of those, it wouldn’t be such a tiny Desk concert, now, would it?

recentItems.title: Gracie's Corner: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Alanté Serene | November 16, 2026
The first time I heard a Gracie's Corner song, it stopped me in my tracks. The beat cranked so hard that I rushed over to see what my niece was watching. "This can't be for toddlers," I thought. Turns out I was being introduced to a platform that is educational, empowering and, yes, age-appropriate. It's not often that an animated series makes music that grown folks actually enjoy, but this family production out of Houston, Texas, has changed the way so many hear nursery rhymes.

Graceyn Hollingsworth, the inspiration and voice behind Gracie, came to the Tiny Desk properly prepped. The series was created with Graceyn's parents, Dr. Javoris Hollingsworth and Dr. Arlene Gordon-Hollingsworth, when they noticed a lack of Black representation in children's programming. Both parents watched proudly from the Tiny Desk sidelines as 13-year-old Graceyn led the band through a high-energy, beat-heavy set that had kids and adults dancing and singing along.

The little ones could hardly contain themselves when the costumed versions of Gracie and Zyron joined for "Phonics Song," "Elephant Song" and "Veggie Dance." Then Houston rap legend Paul Wall popped up for "Wheels on the Bus (H-Town Remix)," and the grown-ups got just as loud. By the end, the whole room was smiling and moving, soaking in a moment that showed what learning, inclusion, hard work and Black girl magic look like when they come together.

recentItems.title: Robyn: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Dora Levite, Lars Gotrich | November 12, 2026
There is so much humanity within Robyn's music — not just longing and heartbreak, but absurdity, the connections and contradictions that are all part of life's panoply. Her crystal-clear voice, honed over 30 years, sparkles in this Tiny Desk.

Every choice here is a tender one, down to the teardrop glued to her cheek. Every move is confident, yet comes from a place of vulnerability. Most of these arrangements play up the quiet desperation in her outsized songs, though on "Ever Again," Robyn pulls off a magic trick by inviting us into the conversation, opening a broken heart to defiant resilience. "Light Up," in particular, sounds revelatory, a glitchy synth banger reborn as a piano ballad. "I was looking at you like a mirror," she sings with a catch in her throat, like an old memory surfacing for a split second, as she builds to a moment of emotional release.

Robyn was 16 years old when "Show Me Love" appeared on her debut album, Robyn Is Here. "For me, this is where it all started, in a way," she tells the audience, understating the foundational impact the hit would have on late-'90s pop. Behind the Desk, its lite new jack swing slows to something more spacious and reflective, if no less flirtatious. She lets the music age with her.

If softness is the move throughout this set, "Sucker for Love" shakes loose the feels and revels in the sensuality that permeates this year's Sexistential. Her steely blue eyes dare us, and her, not to hold back from expressions of desire — to trust in the mess and find something real.

recentItems.title: Fat Joe: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Bobby Carter | November 5, 2026
When Fat Joe walked into NPR headquarters, he intended to shake the table (or desk, in this case). He wanted to "touch the third rail," meaning it would be anything but your typical Tiny Desk concert, and the audience would be treated to a new level of spontaneity. The way this show is treacherous and unpredictable, yet lands on incredibly solid footing, directly reflects how Joey Crack's career has survived and thrived for over 30 years.

In the five years since his Tiny Desk (home) concert, Joe Cartagena has continued to reinvent himself, leaning into his polarizing takes and storytelling as an internet personality, writing a book and, more recently, co-hosting the popular Joe and Jada podcast with another Tiny Desk alum, Jadakiss. Fat Joe's music has remained the driving force, with consistent album output and hit records.

For his Tiny Desk, the Bronx emcee flexes the benefits of loyalty and longevity, inviting a laundry list of guest appearances from Remy Ma, Stove God Cooks, Stevie Mackey, Dre (from the production duo Cool & Dre) and Jadakiss, in support of career-spanning set list and songs from his latest album, Organized Rhyme.

recentItems.title: Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Robin Hilton | November 2, 2026
It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems.

Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano. 

The members are all smiles here, even as they sing about faded dreams ("Casio"), dead-end infatuations ("Someday, Somewhere") and the struggle to hold on when everything falls apart ("The Wave"). The most animated and infectious moment arrives about halfway through the set, as the group showcases its stunning six-part harmonies on the 2025 single "Keep Me Satisfied," before closing with a moody, slow-burning take on 2023's breakout song, "Back on 74."

recentItems.title: Richard O'Brien's 'The Rocky Horror Show': Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Mitra I. Arthur | October 30, 2026
If you happened to be in the NoMa area of Washington, D.C., on the right evening in October, you may have seen some interesting characters entering the NPR offices: people dressed in fishnets and corsets, perhaps a few maid costumes; maybe a '50s-style greaser or a bespectacled super-nerd. When you welcome the Broadway revival of Richard O'Brien's The Rocky Horror Show, it's only fitting to fill the audience with Frank-N-Furters, Magentas, Eddies, Riff Raffs, Brads, Janets, and various other creatures of the night.

For over 50 years, The Rocky Horror Show (and its film adaptation, The Rocky Horror Picture Show), with its catchy songs and off-kilter camp storytelling, has provided both passionate fans and the uninitiated with a space to find community, to be seen, and to feel free. To match the spirit of the show, we transformed the Tiny Desk into our own version of the Frankenstein Place.

Our strange journey into Rocky Horror begins with "Science Fiction Double Feature," as Anania's effervescent vocals welcome us to the sci-fi B-movie world. "Over at the Frankenstein Place" features Lorna Courtney and Kevin McHale perfectly inhabiting the naive sweetness of young lovers Brad and Janet, while Andres Quintero's vocal timbre provides a harbinger of what thrills await the pair. The electric, '50s-tinged rocker "Hot Patootie" is performed to thrilling effect by George Salazar, punctuated by Lynn Ligammari's grooving saxophone. Jake Shears' performance of Frank-N-Furter's ballad "I'm Going Home" is captivating and heartbreaking.

I confess one of my not-so-secret goals for this show was to see an audience full of NPR staff and guests jumping to the left, stepping to the right … you know the rest. After all, what would a Rocky Horror Tiny Desk be without a performance of the show's most fun and infectious tune? Lucky for us, we'll never know. So limber up, put your hands on your hips, knees tight, and join the in-room audience in doing "The Time Warp."

recentItems.title: CMAT: Tiny Desk Concert
recentItems.description:
Elle Mannion | October 27, 2026
From top to (cheeky) bottom, CMAT’s Tiny Desk has it all: captivating stage presence, sharp songwriting, vocal range, a great band and comedic timing.

Across this set, the Irish singer-songwriter offers a refreshing perspective for country music. On the pop hit “Take a Sexy Picture of Me,” she uses humor as a response to cruel comments she’s received about her appearance. On “When a Good Man Cries,” CMAT deals with the guilt of hurting an ex who was good to her; as the song builds, she raises her hands above her head as her powerhouse vocals harmonize with the band and repeats, “Kyrie eleison,” which translates to “Lord, have mercy.” “I Wanna Be a Cowboy, Baby!” is a classic-sounding, country two-step about social anxiety and emotional detachment.

CMAT closes with a song that she doesn’t usually play live. She spends most of “Lord, Let That Tesla Crash” with her eyes closed, sitting inside the devastating words written in memory of Jo Rose, a musician from Manchester, England who died in 2024. But as she opens herself up in the final moments, she lets out one last cackle, knowing that her “gorgeous egomaniac” friend “would get a kick out of this.”
